title: MCP 2026-07-28 Spec: Stateless Core, MCP Apps & Tasks
content:
## Overview

The Model Context Protocol steering group shipped a release candidate for the **2026-07-28 revision** of the spec — the largest rewrite since MCP launched in November 2024. The headline change: the protocol core moves from stateful to **stateless**, which changes how servers scale and how clients authenticate. Beta SDKs are available now for Python, TypeScript, Go, and C#.

---

## Stateless Core

Prior MCP revisions required an `initialize` handshake that established a protocol-level session, which then had to be tracked for the lifetime of the connection. That meant a remote MCP server behind a load balancer needed sticky sessions, a shared session store, or deep packet inspection at the gateway just to route follow-up requests to the right backend instance.

The 2026-07-28 revision **removes the initialize handshake and the protocol-level session entirely**. Every request is now self-contained — it carries whatever context it needs rather than relying on server-side session state. Practical effect: a stateless MCP server can sit behind a plain round-robin load balancer with no sticky routing, which is a meaningfully simpler deployment story for anyone running MCP servers at scale (this matters for the kind of multi-connector setups Claude Code and Claude.ai use — Slack, Gmail, Google Drive, GitHub, etc.).

---

## New Capabilities

- **MCP Apps** — servers can now deliver interactive HTML interfaces that the host renders inside a sandboxed iframe. This lets an MCP server ship a small UI (a form, a chart, a config panel) instead of being limited to text/JSON tool results.
- **Tasks** — a stateless model for long-running work. Instead of holding a session open while a slow operation (a large crawl, a batch export) completes, a client can kick off a task and poll or receive a callback, without any server-side session to keep alive.

---

## Enterprise-Managed Authorization

The **Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA)** extension, previously experimental, was promoted to **stable**. It gives organizations a centralized way to control which MCP servers their users/agents can reach, enforced through their existing identity provider (SSO/IdP) rather than per-server credential management. This targets the same problem Claude Code's connector permissions (`ListConnectors`, `SuggestConnectors`) solve at the client level, but pushes enforcement to the org's IdP so it applies uniformly across every MCP client an employee uses, not just one tool.

---

## Breaking Changes & Migration

- Servers built against the 2026-07-28 revision **may not work with older (pre-stateless) clients**, and vice versa — this is an explicit protocol break, not a soft deprecation.
- The spec authors have also established a **formal deprecation policy** for the first time: once a feature is marked deprecated, it must keep working for at least 12 months before removal. This is new — earlier MCP revisions had no committed deprecation window.
- Server and client authors are expected to negotiate protocol version during connection setup and fall back gracefully where possible.

---

## Why It Matters

MCP shipped in November 2024 as a standard way to plug tools and data sources into Claude and other MCP-compatible clients (see [Tool Use & Agents](tool-use-and-agents)). Two years in, the stateful session model was becoming the main scaling bottleneck for hosted MCP servers serving many concurrent agents. This revision is effectively MCP admitting it needs to look more like a normal stateless web API (closer to REST/JSON-RPC-over-HTTP conventions) to support the current scale of agentic deployments, while adding EMA and MCP Apps to catch up with enterprise and UI-embedding needs that came up repeatedly as adoption grew.
